title: Macquarie Group dumps KPMG from audit contract
full_text:
Macquarie Group has announced it will drop KPMG as an auditor, amid an ongoing scandal relating to its handling of confidential information.
Macquarie announced on Wednesday afternoon that its board held concerns over the firm's auditing practices, amid ongoing scrutiny of KPMG.
"The decision follows continued scrutiny of KPMG Australia's audit practice, including information exposed by the Parliamentary Joint Committee on Corporations and Financial Services," the statement said.
"It also follows Macquarie's formal enquiries of KPMG to consider its capacity to deliver the audit, as well as the nature and impact of ongoing issues at KPMG Australia."
The board said it would instead recommend incumbent auditor PwC auditor at the company's annual general meeting.
KPMG also released a statement acknowledging the decision.
"While disappointed by the outcome, KPMG respects the decision taken by Macquarie," the statement read.
KPMG chief executive John Sams said Macquarie's announcement was "a clear reminder that the consequences of our past failings are real".
"Rebuilding trust will require sustained action, transparency and time. I am committed to leading this change with honesty, transparency and urgency," he said.
Whistleblower raised concerns 'through the appropriate channels'
KPMG has faced scrutiny over the alleged misuse of client data and misconduct after a whistleblower brought their complaints forward in 2024.
Public documents released by the parliamentary committee, shared with the whistleblower's consent, detail the nature of the allegations, including claims the firm mishandled the whistleblower's initial complaints.
The whistleblower told the committee said they attempted to address the issues with the KPMG partners, the head of audit, senior leadership and independent directors, before reaching out to KPMG International's whistleblower hotline and global leadership.
They ultimately turned to ASIC and Senator Deborah O'Neill, which triggered the parliamentary inquiry.
Among the more serious allegations were claims KPMG had stored confidential board papers and "used in the pursuit of major audit tenders," the statement read.
The whistleblower told the committee these were not "minor employment matters" and further claimed in one instance partners offered access to clients internal audit papers along to with a Telstra-issued laptop.
The next public hearing is slated for September 4, 2026, in Sydney.
